Senses.Explanation: A proper name, literally "Mighty-Sound King" (威音王), occurring 487 times in 171 allowlisted texts. The extended form "Mighty-Sound King Buddha" (威音王佛) occurs 80 times. Chan records most often place the name in temporal and spatial formulas: "before Mighty-Sound King" (威音王已前, 181 occurrences), "after Mighty-Sound King" (威音王已後, 33), and "the far side of Mighty-Sound King" (威音王那畔, 17). In the Nanquan-Huangbo exchange, Huangbo says he followed the Way "before Mighty-Sound King"; Nanquan answers, "you are still a descendant of old Master Wang" (猶是王老師兒孫在), using Nanquan's surname Wang in the reply. In the Yongjia record, Xuanze says, "before Mighty-Sound King, it is acceptable; after Mighty-Sound King, awakening by oneself without a teacher is entirely the way of outsiders" (威音王已前即得，威音王已後無師自悟，盡是天然外道). Xuedou records "awakening by oneself without a teacher before Mighty-Sound King" as "the second phrase" (是第二句). A late Sanfeng record supplies an explicit internal gloss: "Mighty-Sound King is outside form and sound, not yet set out in records, without evidence to examine—the highest matter before writing" (威音王者，形聲之外，未有出載，無所考據，文字以前最上事也). This entry reports the proper name and the corpus's formulas without adding another framework.
Senses.Note: Dahui also reports and rejects a contemporary equation: people "close the brows and shut the eyes" and call that "news from the far side of Mighty-Sound King, from before father and mother were born," also calling it "silent yet constantly illuminating" (閉眉合眼，謂之威音王那畔父母未生時消息，亦謂之默而常照). This is included as Dahui's critical report, not adopted as the headword's meaning. The Huangbo-Nanquan wording is a two-speaker case and is therefore not assigned to either speaker in the occurrence link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 檗曰。威音王已前。師曰。猶是王老師兒孫在。下去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Nanquan Puyuan's section of the Compendium of Five Lamps. Huangbo says, "before Mighty-Sound King"; Nanquan replies, "you are still a descendant of old Master Wang—get down." MasterName is null because the headword occurs in Huangbo's turn inside a two-speaker exchange governed by Nanquan's section.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云威音王已前南泉云猶是王老師孫在師便下去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Huangbo Wanling Record's independent witness of the Nanquan-Huangbo exchange: Huangbo says "before Mighty-Sound King" and Nanquan answers that he is still old Master Wang's descendant. The two-speaker occurrence remains unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 威音王已前即得，威音王已後無師自悟，盡是天然外道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Yongjia Xuanjue section of the Linked Lamps, Xuanze speaks this line to Yongjia: "before Mighty-Sound King, it is acceptable; after Mighty-Sound King, awakening by oneself without a teacher is entirely the way of outsiders." The speaker is Xuanze, not the section master, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 閉眉合眼。謂之威音王那畔父母未生時消息。亦謂之默而常照。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Dahui Zonggao's reply to Zhang Anguo. Dahui critically lists people who "close the brows and shut the eyes" and call this "news from the far side of Mighty-Sound King, from before father and mother were born," also calling it "silent yet constantly illuminating."

Occurrences.Kwic: 威音王已前無師自悟。是第二句。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Xuedou Chongxian's own record: "awakening by oneself without a teacher before Mighty-Sound King is the second phrase."

Occurrences.Kwic: 威音王者，形聲之外，未有出載，無所考據，文字以前最上事也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct self-definition in the Sanfeng Zang record: "Mighty-Sound King is outside form and sound, not yet set out in records, without evidence to examine—the highest matter before writing." No roster-safe master value is used for this late record.

Senses.Explanation: To keep or observe binding precepts. The compound appears 460 times in 154 allowlisted texts and can straightforwardly appraise a monk: one master calls a boy ‘only a monk who has kept the precepts for one or two lives’ (只是一兩生持戒僧), while a biography praises a master over eighty for keeping the precept rules as strictly as a novice monk. It also establishes public accountability: a master asks, ‘You are a precept-keeping person; why do you not observe the monastic code?’ (你是持戒人，為什不守清規？). The Chan record then tests what keeping amounts to. Huineng’s no-form verse asks, ‘the mind level, why labor at keeping precepts?’ (心平何勞持戒), pairing it with ‘conduct straight, what use is cultivating Chan?’ Juelang calls receiving precepts an initial gate, says early keeping may not yet be fully according to rule, and elsewhere says receiving without being able to keep is an offense. These passages retain keeping as appraised, long-term, and answerable conduct while placing effortful keeping beside level mind and straight conduct.
Senses.Note: Flyswatter-test deviation: keeping precepts remains a hard conduct predicate, but the records place effortful keeping beside level mind and straight conduct and test claims that reception is unnecessary. Exact count: 460 hits in 154 files.

Occurrences.Kwic: 心平何勞持戒，行直何用修禪！
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huineng pairs the question about laboring at precept-keeping with straight conduct.

Occurrences.Kwic: 也只是一兩生持戒僧。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master appraises a boy as a monk of only one or two lives’ precept-keeping.

Occurrences.Kwic: 正以受戒為人定慧之初門。最初持戒，未必能盡如法，未必能盡精純。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Juelang calls reception an initial gate and says first efforts at keeping may not yet be fully according to rule or pure.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師道風高峻，海內咸稱古佛。年八十餘，嚴持戒法，如新學比丘。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A biography records strict precept-keeping into old age, compared with a novice monk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 你是持戒人，為什不守清規？曰：和尚莫以罪罪人好！
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public exchange holds a precept-keeper answerable to the community's monastic code.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to examine and awaken; in the Chan records, to come to understand. The term occurs 229 times in 98 allowlisted texts, chiefly as a biographical result clause. A monk is told to wash his bowl and suddenly understands; Shigong cannot bring himself to shoot Mazu and understands; a layman is asked whether he understands and suddenly does; and Daowu hears a spirit-medium's song and suddenly understands. An instructional record also says there must be a basis for understanding and warns against stopping after grasping a few fixed phrases. The term records the narrator's or teacher's verdict that understanding occurred; the word itself adds no account of what was understood.
Senses.Note: One verbal event across sudden and unmodified forms. The various occasions—speech, question, action, or heard song—are causes supplied by their narratives, not separate senses of the word.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。洗鉢盂去。其僧忽然省悟。上堂。纔有是非。紛然失心。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The wash-your-bowl case uses the term as its narrated result.

Occurrences.Kwic: 石鞏慧藏禪師初為獵人射鹿，因遇馬，祖令自射，無下手處，省悟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Shigong's biography reports understanding when he cannot shoot Mazu.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。還會麼。居士忽然省悟。有頌云。心鏡從來瑩。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public question to a layman is followed by the narrator's verdict and a verse.

Occurrences.Kwic: 聞巫者樂神云：識神無。忽然省悟。後參前關南，印其所解。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Daowu's biography reports sudden understanding on hearing a song, followed by confirmation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 須知有省悟之由若真實叅學但恁麼看據現定會些子言句便休也在
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An instructional record contrasts a basis for understanding with stopping at a few grasped phrases.

Senses.Explanation: An old (老) monk (僧): “old monk.” The form occurs 11,424 times in 388 allowlisted texts. Its characteristic Chan deployment is a monk's humble first-person self-reference, conventionally translated “this old monk” and grammatically serving as “I” or “me.” A master speaks of “this old monk's place,” redirects a public interview by saying “this old monk is hard of hearing; ask loudly,” recalls receiving a shout, or addresses the assembly at his final meeting. The same noun phrase also refers in narration to an old monk: Wuzhuo meets one, a raised case begins with an old monk carried by two disciples, and a record introduces “an old monk named Puhui.” Speaker self-reference, third-person reference, and definiteness are contextual readings of the same human-role noun, not different things.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide human-role sense. Render it as “this old monk” when a speaker uses it for himself and “an/the old monk” in third-person narration. Do not restore the former article/deixis split. A separate local sense below is retained only because that passage explicitly uses the source term (老僧) for a different referent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。汝道老僧即今在什麼處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Nanyang Huizhong tests a visitor by asking where 'this old monk' is now. It is a narrated two-person encounter, so the speaker field remains null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 佛法不是小事。老僧昔再蒙馬大師一喝。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Baizhang Huaihai's explicit section, Baizhang uses the phrase for himself while recalling a shout from Master Ma.

Occurrences.Kwic: 老僧穩坐更有道流來相見時我盡辨了也
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji alternates 'this old monk' and the first-person pronoun 'I' in one clause, directly displaying the self-referential reading.

Occurrences.Kwic: 到山下投一寺宿遇一老僧祗待次問無著曰
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a raised Wuzhuo encounter, the narrator says that Wuzhuo met an old monk who received him.

Occurrences.Kwic: 白晝閑眠一老僧
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A descriptive verse says, 'An old monk sleeps at leisure in daylight,' an ordinary third-person noun phrase.

Occurrences.Kwic: 老僧者裏即易見難識。若能會得，天下橫行。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The productive phrase 'at this old monk's place' marks the speaker's present teaching locus.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「如何是和尚家風？」師云：「老僧耳背，高聲問。」僧再問
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Inside a public interview the master says, 'This old monk is hard of hearing; ask loudly,' redirecting the exchange.

Occurrences.Kwic: 老僧今日火風相逼，特與諸人相見。諸人還見麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: At a final meeting, the speaker uses 'this old monk' for himself while saying that fire and wind press upon him.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有一老僧命二徒肩輿而行，中途有人問云：『既是和尚，為甚麼抬和尚？』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A raised case opens with an indefinite third-person old monk being carried in a litter by two disciples.

Occurrences.Kwic: 石霜山中有一老僧，號曰普會。雖有道行，不為世人之所欽奉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The record introduces a specific old monk by name, Puhui, confirming the ordinary human noun outside speaker self-reference.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the pre-cosmic self, a local defined referent
Senses.Explanation: A local request-for-instruction passage explicitly says, “Understanding the self before the empty eon is termed the old monk.” Here the source term (老僧) names the “self before the empty eon,” not a human monk and not merely another reading of the ordinary noun. The definition belongs to this passage alone; it is not projected onto the thousands of ordinary first- and third-person uses.
Senses.Note: Local, provisional sense required by the explicit “is termed” formula (謂之). Keep MasterName null unless the speaker is independently identified on the roster. Do not generalize this sense corpus-wide.

Occurrences.Kwic: 明得空劫自己謂之老僧，也出不得者裏。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The local commentator explicitly defines understanding the self before the empty eon as 'the old monk.' No exact roster attribution is established.

Senses.PreferredTarget: an old woman's concern is pressing
AlternateTargets: old-woman concern pressed to the utmost
pressing concern like an old woman's
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "an old woman's concern is pressing": old woman or granny (老婆) plus the concern being urgent or pressed hard (心切). The phrase occurs 270 times in 129 allowlisted texts. It is a predicate applied to a speaker's insistent words or actions toward someone else, not the name of an inner state or a sentimental ideal. In the Linji–Huangbo–Dayu case, Dayu says Huangbo's old-woman concern was so pressing that "for you he exhausted himself completely" (為汝得徹困); when Linji returns, he says it was "only because the old-woman concern was pressing" (祇為老婆心切). In another exchange, a layman calls Huitang's concern pressing and Huitang replies, "I only want you to arrive home" (秖要公到家耳). The records thus show the idiom through predicates, agents, and replies rather than through a modern emotional gloss.
Senses.Note: The phrase is neither automatically praise nor a guarantee that the action described is harmless. A commentary reports that people call Jinniu's carrying rice and dancing "pressing old-woman concern," then rejects their reading: it is "arsenic soaked in honey to entice people to put it in their mouths" (以蜜浸砒霜誘人下口). Elsewhere the location of Yaoshan's pressing concern is itself made the next interview question: "where is the place of his pressing old-woman concern?" (那裏是他老婆心切處). It can also enter verse, as in "pressing old-woman concern, laughing ha-ha, letting bystanders say long or short" (老婆心切呵呵笑，一任傍人說短長). Common frames include "only because" (只為老婆心切, 24 occurrences; variant 祇為, 7) and "so very" (得恁麼老婆心切, 18). These uses support a forceful relational appraisal while preserving the possibility of criticism.

Occurrences.Kwic: 愚曰：黃檗與麼老婆心切，為汝得徹困，更來這裡問有過無過？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dayu tells Linji that Huangbo's old-woman concern was so pressing that Huangbo exhausted himself completely for him; Dayu then asks why Linji still asks whether he was at fault.

Occurrences.Kwic: 檗見便問：這漢來來去去，有甚了期？師曰：祇為老婆心切。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: On returning, Linji answers Huangbo's complaint about his coming and going: only because the old-woman concern was pressing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 公釋然即拜之曰。和尚得恁麼老婆心切。堂笑曰。秖要公到家耳。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The layman bows and says the teacher's old-woman concern is very pressing; Huitang laughs and replies that he only wants the layman to arrive home.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：藥山老漢得恁老婆心切。進云：且那裏是他老婆心切處？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yaoshan is called an old fellow whose old-woman concern is very pressing; the interlocutor immediately asks where its pressing point is.

Occurrences.Kwic: 人見其自舁飯作舞，多道老婆心切，殊不知以蜜浸砒霜誘人下口。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A corrective use: people call Jinniu's carrying rice and dancing pressing old-woman concern, but the commentator says it is arsenic soaked in honey to entice people to swallow.

Occurrences.Kwic: 老婆心切呵呵笑，一任傍人說短長。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Verse line describing Zhaozhou: pressing old-woman concern, laughing ha-ha, letting bystanders say long or short.

RelatedTerms: exhaust oneself completely for someone (為汝得徹困)
only want you to arrive home (秖要公到家耳)
arsenic soaked in honey (蜜浸砒霜)

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'old-woman Chan.' The expression occurs 211 times in 112 allowed texts and functions as a label applied to sayings, explanations, and handling that records compare with an old woman's solicitous speech. The verbal form 'speak old-woman Chan' (說老婆禪) occurs 55 times in 36 texts. Dahui asks whether the National Teacher's three calls to his attendant may be called 'speaking old-woman Chan, dragging through mud and water' (說老婆禪，拖泥帶水), and elsewhere says that if he had initially spoken old-woman Chan and explained everything to a student, the student would later have cursed him. A later letter contrasts a master's 'pungent handling' (手段辛辣) with people elsewhere who speak old-woman Chan. The label is also attached to actual old-woman encounters: verses call the Chan of the old woman in the Floating Cup case and the old woman on the road to Mount Wutai 'old-woman Chan.' Other records apply it more broadly. A verse calls a line 'old-woman Chan in the great Tang country' (大唐國裏老婆禪), and a case pointer asks whether someone with firm heels would consent to learn old-woman Chan. The term is therefore an attested appraisal label rather than the name of a separate lineage: records apply it approvingly, critically, and ironically to different sayings and encounters.
Senses.Note: The entry retains the literal gendered image because the corpus repeatedly connects the compound with an old woman's speech and with the broader collocation 'old-woman heart' (老婆心), which occurs 706 times in 214 texts; 'old-woman heart is urgent' (老婆心切) occurs 270 times in 129. The exact definition formulas yield two occurrences of 'one who speaks old-woman Chan' (說老婆禪者) and two of 'call it old-woman Chan' (喚作老婆禪), but no stable equation that narrows the label beyond the recorded comparisons and deployments.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如三喚侍者話。喚作說老婆禪拕泥帶水得麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui discusses the National Teacher's three calls to his attendant and asks whether it can be called speaking old-woman Chan and dragging through mud and water.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若使老漢初為渠拕泥帶水說老婆禪。眼開後定罵我無疑。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui says that had he initially dragged through mud and water speaking old-woman Chan for the student, the student would surely have cursed him after his eyes opened.

Occurrences.Kwic: 每服大師手段辛辣，與諸方說老婆禪者迥殊
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A letter praises the recipient's pungent handling as utterly different from those elsewhere who speak old-woman Chan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 今時叢林中聞與麼道，便道說老婆禪。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Collection of the Five Lamps. The speaker reports that people in contemporary communities hear such wording and immediately call it speaking old-woman Chan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 脚跟牢實。肯學老婆禪。透得無巴鼻機關。始見正作家手段。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Book of Serenity pointer. The text asks whether one with firm heels would consent to learn old-woman Chan, then continues with passing through a trackless mechanism and seeing an expert's handling.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大唐國裏老婆禪。今日為君注破了。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's verse calls it old-woman Chan in the great Tang country and says that today it has been annotated through for the listener.
